title: Exam score standardized normal upper tail
scenario_markdown: Scores on a quantitative certification exam are normally distributed with mean $\mu = 70$ points and standard deviation $\sigma = 10$ points ($X \sim N(70, 10^2)$). Find the probability that a randomly selected candidate scores at least 85 points.
assumptions: Standard normal table / CDF symmetry applies

approval.notes: Reviewed derivation: Z = (85 - 70)/10 = 1.50. P(Z >= 1.50) = 1 - Phi(1.50) = 1 - 0.93319 = 0.0668. Verified continuous point probability P(X = 85) = 0.

stages.prompt_markdown: What is the standard score ($Z$-score) corresponding to an exam score of $X = 85$?

options.hint_markdown: Standardization requires dividing the distance from the mean by the standard deviation $\sigma$.
The $Z$-score formula is $\frac{X - \mu}{\sigma}$, where $X = 85$ is above the mean.

stages.explanation_markdown: $Z = \frac{X - \mu}{\sigma} = \frac{85 - 70}{10} = +1.50$, indicating a score 1.5 standard deviations above the mean.

stages.prompt_markdown: Find the probability of scoring at least 85 points: $P(X \ge 85) = P(Z \ge 1.50) = 1 - \Phi(1.50)$. Enter as a decimal or percentage rounded to four decimal places.
stages.explanation_markdown: From standard normal tables, $\Phi(1.50) \approx 0.9332$. Therefore, $P(Z \ge 1.50) = 1 - 0.9332 = 0.0668$ (or $6.68\%$). Excel formula: `=1 - NORM.DIST(85, 70, 10, TRUE)` or `=1 - NORM.S.DIST(1.5, TRUE)`.

stages.prompt_markdown: What is the probability of a candidate scoring *exactly* 85.000 points ($P(X = 85)$)?

options.text_markdown: $P(X = 85) = 0$. For any continuous distribution, the probability of an exact individual value is strictly zero.
$P(X = 85) \approx 0.013$ because that is the height of the normal curve $f(85)$
options.hint_markdown: The height of the curve $f(x)$ represents probability density, not probability. Area under a single point is zero.
An exact point is not a tail region.

stages.explanation_markdown: In all continuous probability models, probability corresponds to area under the density curve. A single exact point has zero width ($dx = 0$), so $P(X = c) = 0$. Curve height $f(85) \approx 0.0130$ is density, not probability.
